extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Shakespeare/literary historians
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing and assembling biographical facts about William Shakespeare, weighing documentary records, publications, contemporary allusions, oral tradition, portraits, and financial/legal evidence. Useful for literary historians judging the reliability and significance of different kinds of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticated facts about Shakespeare's life
rubrics_metrics.description: Such is the very considerable body of authenticated facts about the life of Shakespeare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer documentary, contemporaneous records as primary basis: registrations (Stationers' Hall entries), dedications signed by Shakespeare, Treasurer of the Chamber accounts, parish registers (burials, marriages), deeds, mortgages, court rolls, depositions, and the First Folio's preliminary documents. These authenticated facts form the main skeleton of his career and are given greatest weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemporary allusions and literary references
rubrics_metrics.description: Reminiscences or references to his works are frequent in contemporary literature (e.g., Francis Meres' Palladis Tamia, Barnfield, Weever).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contemporaneous mentions, encomia, and lists of works as evidence for reputation, dating, and attribution of plays/poems. Such allusions corroborate authorship and public standing (e.g., Meres' comparisons and lists of plays). Treat them as valuable corroborative evidence of reputation and output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publications and title-page attributions as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The quarto editions of plays and the appearance of Shakespeare's name on title-pages and the dedications of Venus and Adonis and Lucrece indicate authorship and literary distinction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine publisher records, title-pages, dedications, and frequency/number of editions (e.g., seven editions of Venus, five of Lucrece) as indicators of the author's involvement, control of text, and public success. Note that title-page attributions may be added by publishers (including pirates) and should be cross-checked with other evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and financial records as indicators of status
rubrics_metrics.description: Property purchases (New Place, Blackfriars house), mortgages, acquisitions of tithes, and litigation document Shakespeare's substantial fortune and business engagements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use deeds, conveyances, mortgages, court suits, tax records, and company accounts (e.g., Revels Accounts) to establish economic status, investments, theatre shares, litigation involvement, and social standing. Quantitative details (prices, amounts, dates) allow estimation of income and relative prosperity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signatures and manuscript autographs
rubrics_metrics.description: Of Shakespeare's handwriting nothing that can be called his with complete assurance has survived except six signatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat surviving signatures and legal signatures as limited but important autograph evidence; examine spelling variants and script style. Recognize that most play manuscripts are lost, so autograph evidence is sparse and must be contextualized with other records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portraits and likeness evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Our knowledge of Shakespeare's personal appearance is far from definite: the Stratford bust, Droeshout engraving, and various portraits (Ely Palace, Chandos, Garrick bust, Kesselstadt death-mask) have varying claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate portraits by provenance and pedigree; consider the Droeshout engraving as likely based on a portrait but note the engraver's youth. No portrait is without flaw—assess color, date, and chain of custody before accepting likeness as authentic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oral tradition and anecdote (traditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A large mass of tradition, of less than legal validity but much of it of a high degree of probability, has come down to us (sources include Fuller, Aubrey, Rowe, Ward, D'Avenant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use oral traditions, memoirs, and anecdotes cautiously: they can supply temperament, habit, and color (e.g., convivial tendencies, deer-stealing stories, acting reminiscences) but often contain inaccuracies and embellishments. Consider proximity of informants and corroboration before relying on them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provenance and temporal proximity of sources
rubrics_metrics.description: The credibility of accounts depends on their temporal and personal proximity (e.g., Fuller had access to oral tradition from men who knew Shakespeare; Rowe used Betterton's material from actors who had been colleagues).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give greater weight to sources closer in time or connected to eyewitnesses/participants. Trace chains of transmission (actor recollections, prompter Downes, letters) to assess likely reliability and spot secondary amplification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative economic/contextual data for inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparisons with contemporary practice (e.g., managers paid £5–£11 for plays, actors' salaries, share receipts from the Globe) are used to estimate Shakespeare's income and social position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use market norms, average payments, recorded salaries, and company share values to infer likely earnings and economic standing. Such comparative data provide context when direct figures are absent or fragmentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Official patents, court recognition, and public honors
rubrics_metrics.description: Royal patent of May 19, 1603 (making the Lord Chamberlain's Company the King's servants) and records of performances before the court document official recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat royal patents, court performance records, rewards, and ceremonial records (e.g., procession cloaks, Revels payments) as strong evidence of formal standing, patronage, and institutional position within the theatrical world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemporaries' critical commentary as artistic evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments by Ben Jonson, Webster, Meres, and others offer judgment on Shakespeare's style and strengths (e.g., 'mellifluous and honey-tongued', comparisons to Plautus and Seneca).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contemporaneous critical remarks for qualitative assessment of literary qualities, genres of strength (comedy vs tragedy), and reputation among peers. Distinguish praise useful for artistic evaluation from partisan or anecdotal remarks.
